children: IBM is betting that the mainframe--its flagship infrastructure product since 1964--will remain integral to enterprises' technology stacks even as customers increasingly focus their budgets on artificial-intelligence.

Since the company warned in July that a shortfall in mainframe dealmaking hurt its infrastructure and software segments in the second quarter, investors and analysts have been debating whether AI could render the decades-old mainframe business a dinosaur. IBM is maintaining that the second-quarter shortfall was transitory.
"We do not see anyone getting off of our mainframe platform, and therefore the associated mainframe software stack on top of it," Chief Financial Officer Jim Kavanaugh said in an interview.

IBM's mainframes are large, on-premises computers designed to continuously run enterprise software and process transactions, particularly in industries like finance or retail that need to rapidly handle large amounts of data and operations. IBM said its newest mainframes can also process 450 billion AI inferences per day.

The company said that two-thirds of the mainframe deals that failed to close in the second quarter came through in the third quarter, with more expected to follow. IBM's third-quarter results, released Wednesday, showed 4% revenue growth in the infrastructure segment to $3.71 billion, ahead of analyst expectations.

Revenue from transaction processing software, which reflects financial transactions and other operations processed through the mainframe, rose 9%. Kavanaugh said that only 20% to 30% of the growth in transaction processing revenue can be credited to the delayed deals, with the rest representing net new business.

The third-quarter print "underscores the strategic relevance of our mainframe platform," Kavanaugh said, noting that the platform is in use by 45 of the top 50 banks, four of the top five airlines, and seven of the top ten retailers.

"Our mainframe right now, it's the most reliable, secure, and scalable architecture in the world. That's why it runs 70% of the world's transaction volumes," Kavanaugh said. "We have the ultimate confidence in the innovation value that we built into this and what its relevancy is in an AI world."

The company is roughly halfway through the current cycle for its latest generation of mainframes, known as z17. A strong mainframe cycle is a crucial ingredient for IBM to hit its target of 5% revenue growth in constant currency next year, Morgan Stanley said in a Thursday note.
Kavanaugh said that already, the new mainframe cycle is tracking around 125% of the previous z16 cycle, which itself was a record-setter for IBM.

He added that IBM's decision to lift the low end of its software guidance for the rest of the year to 7% from 6% should build confidence that the second-quarter performance was deferred rather than destroyed demand.
"If we felt that this was demand destruction, we wouldn't have changed the guidance," Kavanaugh said.
